\chapter{Para Mí --- The Pronouns That Stand on Their Own}
\label{ch:para-mi}
\hlchaptermodality{246}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use a pronoun after a preposition.}

I can use a pronoun after a preposition.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[para mí]{para mí — the pronouns that stand on their own}

\label{lesson:ES-C64-para-mi}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{me} and \emph{te} — the little object pronouns that lean on a verb: \emph{me llamo}, \emph{te quiero}.

Put a preposition in front and they change shape.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: after a preposition}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{El café es} \emph{\textbf{para mí}}. — The coffee is for me.
\end{quote}

Say them: \emph{para} \emph{\textbf{mí}}. \emph{Para} \emph{\textbf{ti}}. \emph{Para} \emph{\textbf{él}}, \emph{para} \emph{\textbf{ella}}.

Only the first two persons actually change. From \emph{él} onward the form is the same one you already use as a subject — which is why this list is shorter to learn than it looks.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Now the accent on \emph{\textbf{mí}}, and it is the kind you have met before: one that tells two identical words apart.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{mi} & \textbf{my} — \emph{mi café} \\
\emph{\textbf{mí}} & \textbf{me}, after a preposition — \emph{para mí} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Same letters, same sound, different jobs — so Spanish marks the stressed one, exactly as it marks \emph{tú} against \emph{tu} and \emph{él} against \emph{el}.

And \emph{ti} has \textbf{no} accent, which looks inconsistent and is not: there is no other \emph{ti} to confuse it with. The mark is only ever spent where something needs separating.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{para mí}, \emph{para ti}, \emph{para él}
  \item \emph{mi café}, then \emph{para mí}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which \emph{mi} carries the accent? (The one meaning \textbf{me}, after a preposition.)

And why has \emph{ti} none? (Nothing to \textbf{separate} it from.)
\end{tcolorbox}
